blocks.text: 1. Dynamic Routing

blocks.alt: A query goes through a router to path A or path B

blocks.text: Multi-Agent Systems introduced a coordinator deciding which specialist handles which piece of a task. Dynamic Routing, choosing which agent or path to use per query at runtime, names the general mechanism that coordinator decision actually is.
It inspects the incoming query first, then sends it down the specific path built for that kind of query.
2. Fixed Path Versus Routed Decision

blocks.alt: A fixed path is compared against a routed decision

blocks.text: A system with one fixed path sends every query through the identical sequence, unlike the fixed pipeline versus agent decisions distinction drawn in Agentic RAG.
Dynamic routing instead inspects the query and picks a path matched to it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Architecture","How the path is chosen"],"rows":[["Fixed path","Same sequence for every query, no inspection"],["Dynamic routing","Query inspected first, path chosen to match"]]}

blocks.text: 3. A Classifier Decides The Destination

blocks.alt: A query goes through a classifier to a destination

blocks.text: A lightweight classifier labels the incoming query before any real work begins, the same idea as classifying query complexity first in Adaptive RAG.
That label determines which agent, tool, or pipeline path actually handles it.
4. Routing Between Specialist Agents

blocks.alt: A query routes to agent A or agent B

blocks.text: Dynamic routing is the concrete mechanism a coordinator uses to pick which specialist handles a query, connecting back to one generalist agent versus several specialists in Multi-Agent Systems.
The routing decision and the coordinator's job are the same thing.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A coordinator agent is performing dynamic routing every time it decides which specialist agent should handle an incoming query, the same mechanism just applied at the agent layer.

blocks.text: 5. Routing Between Retrieval Strategies
A simple factual query can route to naive retrieval while a complex one routes to multi-hop retrieval, the same kind of judgment call as recognizing when Self-RAG is worth its training requirement.
Routing applies just as well beneath the agent layer, to the retrieval strategy itself.

blocks.text: 6. Fallback Paths For Unclear Queries

blocks.alt: An unclear query goes down a fallback path

blocks.text: A query the classifier cannot confidently label still needs somewhere to go.
A default fallback path handles ambiguous or unclassified queries safely.
7. Misrouting Sends A Query Down The Wrong Path

blocks.alt: Misrouting sends a query down the wrong path

blocks.text: A wrong routing decision sends the query down a path never built to handle it, the same propagation risk as an error in an early hop in Multi-Hop RAG.
The rest of that path's processing is wasted on a mismatched query.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A complex multi-hop question misrouted to the simple, single-pass retrieval path wastes every downstream step on a path never designed for that query, the same propagation risk described in Multi-Hop RAG.

blocks.text: 8. The Router Is Its Own Lightweight Component
The classifier making the routing decision should stay fast and cheap, the same principle behind the grader being its own small model in Corrective RAG.
It runs before any of the heavier, specialized work even begins.
9. Recognizing When Dynamic Routing Earns Its Classification Step

blocks.alt: Diverse query types point toward dynamic routing

blocks.text: A system facing several distinct query types benefits from routing.
A system facing only one uniform query type, by contrast, does not need a routing step at all.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Building a fixed pipeline for a system that actually faces several distinct query types.
Forgetting a fallback path for queries the classifier cannot confidently label.
Using an expensive, heavyweight model for the routing decision itself.
Treating a coordinator agent's specialist selection as unrelated to dynamic routing in general.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Dynamic routing chooses which agent or path to use per query at runtime.
A fixed path sends every query through the same sequence; routing inspects the query first.
A lightweight classifier labels the query, and that label determines the path taken.
A multi-agent coordinator's specialist selection is dynamic routing applied at the agent layer.
Routing applies beneath the agent layer too, choosing between retrieval strategies directly.
A default fallback path is needed for queries the classifier cannot confidently label.
A wrong routing decision wastes the entire downstream path on a mismatched query.
The router itself should stay fast and cheap, since it runs before any heavier specialized work.
